But to do that, we need to pick out a persona cuz we can't talk about menopause and muscle growth on the same landing page above the fold. Okay? We need to pick one. And so, we want to drive the menopause persona to a menopause related PDP that talks about all the benefits and speaks to that individual. And then we have a muscle building PDP. and we drive this two separate landing pages. Same thing for the offer. The offer is the obvious one. Obviously, if you change the offer, you need to go to a different PDP because the offer is different, right? If you're doing like a bundle versus a single product versus a different product entirely, needs a unique PDP. Most people don't mess that up. Uh angle is also important. So, this is if we're leaning into different unique mechanisms. Creatine is a good one, which is that we can lean into creatine's cognitive benefits or we can lean into creatine's muscle recovery benefits. Yes, you could stack them on the one landing page. You could say creatine cognitive benefits, muscle benefits, this benefit, but generally you will get better conversion rates and better continuity on the landing page if you can keep the angle the same. And this becomes really important in supplements because almost every supplement can be spun into 15 different angles. Okay, you can say collagen is for 15 different things. Now, the reason why a lot of supplement brands fail when they drive traffic to their Shopify PDP is because they're testing all these different angles on ads, which is great. They're testing collagen for skin health. They're testing collagen for joint health. They're testing collagen against old and younger demographics. But then everyone goes to this landing page that just says collagen. 500 g. Tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick, tick. Benefit number one. benefit number two, benefit number three, benefit number four, benefit number five. So all of these different angles that you were testing here, you have listed as all the benefits of the product. Now what happens from a consumer perspective is I watch an ad, it talks to me about arthritis and I'm like, "Oh, I have arthritis. Let me continue watching." It starts to educate me on the causes of arthritis, the mechanism, and then how collagen in particular helps ease arthritis pain because collagen is the fundamental building block of the connective tissue in the joint. And so, as you increase collagen while supplementing at the same time with vitamin C, it allows for increased uptake and that joint can operate better in less pain. Now, I've watched that ad and I've gone, "Incredible. I'm in constant pain. and I have arthritis. All right, I'm going to click and go through. How can I get my hands on this thing? I then land on this PDP and the ninth point here is arthritis support. And then there are all of these other random things and I go, what? I just watched an ad that told me that this is the solution to my arthritis. But then the landing page is saying this is the solution to everything that exists on the planet. Do I trust this? Do I trust that this supplement that apparently does a million things is going to support the one problem that I actually need it for? or would I prefer to buy a supplement from someone else where the product is only for arthritis support? Obviously, I'm going to go for the supplement which is just dedicated to arthritis support, not all these other things. And so, as a product of that, this converts worse. So, you want specificity over broad application anytime on a landing page and anytime in an ad. Like an ad listing all these benefits isn't going to do well. You need to problem agitate into one and talk to one specific person. Now, let's move into copywriting.
